name: Abaloparatide
lead: Abaloparatide (brand name Tymlos) is a synthetic 34-amino-acid analogue of parathyroid hormone-related protein, PTHrP(1-34), approved in the United States for osteoporosis. Its US label covers postmenopausal women at high fracture risk and men with osteoporosis at high risk, as an injectable bone-forming (anabolic) drug [1][2][24].

The skeleton shapes how a face and body look, and that is why the drug draws attention in looksmaxxing circles. Forum participants discuss bone-forming peptides as a way to build bone density in the jaw and face alongside bonesmashing and orthodontics, to support skeletal development in adolescents, and to strengthen bone during limb lengthening. The chain proponents describe is: stronger or thicker bone, then a more structured facial frame or sturdier healing after leg-lengthening surgery, then a taller or more defined look [4][5][6].

The pivotal phase 3 ACTIVE trial reported that abaloparatide reduced new vertebral fractures versus placebo in postmenopausal women with osteoporosis [3]. Its approved use is osteoporosis; it is not approved for height, skull, jaw or other appearance purposes, and no published study has tested it for those goals. The label carries warnings including osteosarcoma risk and avoidance in patients with open epiphyses [2].

paras: According to Wikipedia, abaloparatide was invented at Ipsen, where it was called BIM-44058 in preclinical work and BA058 in clinical development. Preclinical studies in ovariectomised rats reported increased bone volume, density and microarchitecture, while rodent studies also showed a dose- and time-dependent rise in osteosarcoma incidence; whether this occurs in humans is unknown [24].

A phase 2 trial that began in 2008 enrolled 222 postmenopausal women over 24 weeks and reported bone mineral density gains at two dose levels, with hip effects reported as superior to teriparatide [24][8]. The phase 3 ACTIVE trial (2011-2014) enrolled 2,463 postmenopausal women with a mean age of 69 over 18 months [24][3]. A US application was filed in February 2016 and the drug was approved in April 2017; approval for men followed in December 2022 [24][1]. In Europe the CHMP gave a positive opinion in October 2022 and approval under the name Eladynos followed in December 2022 [24].

Abaloparatide is a 34-amino-acid synthetic peptide with a molar mass of about 3,960 g/mol; it shares about 41% homology with PTH(1-34) and about 76% with PTHrP(1-34) [24]. Radius Health holds patents on the subcutaneous formulation expiring between 2027 and 2028 [24].

The US label indicates abaloparatide for treating postmenopausal women with osteoporosis at high fracture risk or who have failed or are intolerant to other therapy, and to increase bone density in men with osteoporosis under the same conditions [2]. Grokipedia reports FDA approval in April 2017 for women and an extension to men in December 2022, and a lifetime treatment limit of about two years owing to osteosarcoma findings in rodents [1].

No regulatory approval or published study supports appearance uses. Forum participants have proposed it as an adjunct to bonesmashing, as a possible aid to skeletal development during puberty and as a way to strengthen bone during limb lengthening [4][5][6].

According to the label, abaloparatide is an agonist at the PTH1 receptor, activating cAMP signalling and stimulating new bone formation on trabecular and cortical surfaces through osteoblast activity; in rats and monkeys it increased bone mineral density and strength [2]. A 2016 study described its selectivity for particular receptor conformations and the resulting downstream signalling [7]. Forum posts describe it as having more transient signalling and less resorption than PTH analogues, though primary studies address receptor selectivity rather than this comparison [1][7].

Wikipedia describes it as preferentially binding the RG conformation of the PTH1 receptor, which produces a more transient cAMP signal than longer-acting ligands and favours bone formation over resorption [24][7]. Teriparatide, the older drug with which it is often discussed, is the first 34 amino acids of parathyroid hormone; continuous PTH exposure depletes bone, but intermittent daily exposure activates osteoblasts more than osteoclasts, producing net gain [25].

In ACTIVE, a phase 3 double-blind randomised trial in postmenopausal women, abaloparatide 80 micrograms versus placebo was assessed for new vertebral fractures [3]; Grokipedia reports vertebral fracture rates of 0.6% versus 4.2% on placebo over 18 months [1]. An earlier phase 2 study reported effects on bone mineral density in postmenopausal women [8]. Network meta-analyses and reviews of osteoporosis drugs include abaloparatide among agents compared for fracture prevention [9][10][11].

Wikipedia reports that in ACTIVE abaloparatide produced greater bone mineral density increases than placebo and teriparatide, and that in the open-label ACTIVExtend extension (1,139 participants) abaloparatide followed by two years of alendronate reduced vertebral and nonvertebral fractures [24][17]. Further published work includes a comparison with alendronate on fracture risk [18], a phase 3 study in Japanese patients [19], an analysis of the probability of reaching bone-density targets compared with teriparatide [20], and 3D-DXA imaging of cortical bone in the hip [21].

Registered trials include a study in men with osteoporosis (ATOM) [12], a transdermal microneedle-patch phase 3 trial in postmenopausal women [13], a large real-world cardiovascular-safety study [14], and early-effect bone-tissue and surgical-setting studies [15][16]. All study populations are people with osteoporosis or healthy volunteers; no trial in adolescents, for height, or for cosmetic bone changes was found.

The label lists hypersensitivity reactions including anaphylaxis, osteosarcoma risk (avoid in patients with open epiphyses and certain bone diseases), orthostatic hypotension, hypercalcaemia, and hypercalciuria or urolithiasis; the most common adverse reactions are hypercalciuria, dizziness, nausea, headache, palpitations, fatigue and upper abdominal pain [2]. The label states that it is not indicated for females of reproductive potential and that there are no human pregnancy data [2].

A looksmax.org thread proposes combining abaloparatide from informal sources with bonesmashing and orthodontics to build bone mass [4]. Another thread asks whether PTH analogues taken during puberty would have an effect, with replies saying the drugs are bone-anabolic [5]. A third proposes pairing it with limb lengthening to speed or strengthen bone formation [6]. Poster accounts describe obtaining it outside prescription channels; sourcing details are not reproduced here.

A further thread titled around pairing abaloparatide with another drug in a 15-year-old is also part of the discussion [23]. A thread described as a 101 on PTH analogues compares teriparatide and abaloparatide [22].

Teriparatide, sold as Forteo, was approved by the FDA in November 2002 for osteoporosis in men and postmenopausal women at high fracture risk and authorised in the EU in June 2003; biosimilars followed from 2019 [25]. The theoretical osteosarcoma risk seen in rats has not been confirmed in humans, and the FDA has called it extremely rare [25]. Looksmax.org threads often discuss the two PTH analogues together [5][22].

lore.intro: Looksmax.org threads discuss abaloparatide and teriparatide as bone-anabolic drugs that might support bonesmashing, skeletal development or limb lengthening [4][5][6].

claims.claim: Abaloparatide could help rebuild or thicken facial bone alongside bonesmashing and orthodontics.
claims.believers: A forum poster argues that if bone mass is lacking, treating the root with a bone-forming drug makes sense and proposes combining it with controlled bonesmashing [4].
claims.experts: No published study has tested abaloparatide for facial bone change in people without osteoporosis; the approved indication is osteoporosis [2].

claims.claim: Taking a PTH analogue during puberty could affect skeletal growth.
claims.believers: A teenage poster asked whether it would do anything, and repliers described it as the most anabolic bone agent available [5].
claims.experts: The label warns against use in patients with open epiphyses because of osteosarcoma risk, and no trial in adolescents for growth was found [2].

claims.claim: It could speed or strengthen bone formation during limb lengthening.
claims.believers: A poster theorises that PTH-type anabolic agents would shorten recovery and increase bone density after lengthening surgery [6].
claims.experts: Registered trials examine abaloparatide in spinal fusion and knee-surgery settings in osteoporosis patients, not limb lengthening [15][16].

claims.claim: Bone-forming peptides could add bone to the skull or jaw in adults.
claims.believers: Posters on PTH-analogue threads argue that since the drugs build bone in osteoporosis they might thicken facial bone [4][22].
claims.experts: Trials measure spine and hip bone density and fractures in people with osteoporosis; none has measured facial or skull bone in healthy people [3][17].

card.summary: An approved osteoporosis bone-builder that forums speculate about for bonesmashing and lengthening; no appearance trials exist.
card.note: Label warns of osteosarcoma risk and advises against use with open growth plates.

quick.overview:
Abaloparatide is a prescription injectable that stimulates bone formation. It is approved for osteoporosis in postmenopausal women and in men, based on trials that reduced fractures.

Looksmaxxing forums discuss it for bonesmashing, puberty and limb lengthening. No published study tests it for those goals.
quick.mechanism: It activates the PTH1 receptor, increasing osteoblast activity and new bone formation, a pattern described as bone-anabolic.
quick.risks: The label lists osteosarcoma risk, low blood pressure on standing, high calcium, and allergic reactions, and advises avoiding it with open growth plates. It is Rx-only.
